raw_text:
**The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Clinical Narrative Review**

**Introduction**
Sudden cardiac death (SCD) remains a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality worldwide. For decades, transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (TV-ICDs) have served as the standard of care for primary and secondary prevention. However, transvenous leads represent a major point of system vulnerability, frequently associated with both acute and long-term complications, such as pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, venous thrombosis, systemic infection, and lead fracture, which increase in incidence over time [1, 2]. To eliminate the need for intravascular lead placement, an entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed [1]. Since its introduction, the S-ICD has emerged as an established alternative to traditional systems. Contemporary guidelines from the American Heart Association (AHA) / American College of Cardiology (ACC) / Heart Rhythm Society (HRS) [3] and the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [4] now recommend S-ICD therapy as a class I or IIa indication in patients who meet ICD criteria but have no requirement for bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP).

**Early Clinical Foundations and Evolution**
The early feasibility, safety, and efficacy of the S-ICD were established in the pivotal subcutaneous ICD Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) trial [5]. These findings were subsequently reinforced by a pooled analysis of the IDE trial and the European EFFORTLESS registry, which demonstrated excellent shock efficacy and low overall complication rates [6]. Midterm outcomes from the EFFORTLESS registry further confirmed high conversion success rates for spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias in a real-world setting [7]. 

The landmark randomized PRAETORIAN trial provided the first head-to-head comparison between S-ICD and TV-ICD therapies in patients without a pacing indication [8]. Over a median follow-up of 49 months, the S-ICD demonstrated noninferiority to the TV-ICD regarding a composite endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks. Although inappropriate shocks were slightly more frequent in the S-ICD cohort, lead-related complications were significantly reduced. More recently, the UNTOUCHED trial demonstrated that standard programming and enhanced discrimination algorithms significantly reduce inappropriate shock rates to levels comparable to, or even lower than, those of transvenous systems in primary prevention patients with low ejection fractions [9]. However, optimal outcomes depend heavily on operator experience, as a pronounced learning curve has been documented during the adoption of S-ICD technology [10]. To ensure safe sensing and prevent inappropriate shocks, pre-implantation electrocardiographic (ECG) screening is mandatory to verify QRS-to-T-wave ratios across multiple vectors [11]. Long-term clinical comparison data between S-ICD and TV-ICD systems have shown similar survival benefits and overall safety [12].

**Sensing Configurations and Complication Avoidance**
Because S-ICD sensing relies on far-field ECG vectors rather than local intracardiac signals, it is susceptible to cardiac oversensing. Double counting of QRS complexes or T-wave oversensing (TWOS) can result in inappropriate shocks. Several key algorithms have been developed to enhance arrhythmia discrimination and prevent inappropriate therapies caused by supraventricular tachycardia or noise [13]. A significant software enhancement was the introduction of the SMART Pass filter, a high-pass filter designed to reduce the amplitude of T-waves and thus mitigate TWOS [14]. 

Implantation techniques have also evolved. While the device was initially placed using a three-incision surgical technique, a simplified two-incision technique was proposed by Knops et al., which avoids the superior parasternal incision [15]. Real-world, post-market surveillance of the S-ICD, as documented in the S-ICD Post-Approval Study (PAS), confirmed excellent safety and low complication rates [16]. Early performance results from the EFFORTLESS registry underscored the safety of the device across diverse centers [17]. Meanwhile, research into integrating leadless pacing with S-ICD therapy led to the development of communicating wireless systems [18]. To reduce inappropriate shock rates, advanced filtering algorithms were designed and tested [19]. Early Dutch clinical registry cohorts also provided vital real-world safety data on the adoption of the S-ICD [20], while identifying that inappropriate shocks due to oversensing remain a common clinical concern [21]. 

To optimize device positioning and predict defibrillation success without requiring intraoperative defibrillation testing, clinicians developed the quantitative PRAETORIAN score [22]. Long-term follow-up of the two-incision technique has shown it to be safe, highly effective, and cosmetically superior [23]. Recent randomized evidence from the ATLAS trial showed that S-ICD implantation significantly reduces perioperative major lead-related complications compared to TV-ICDs [24]. Furthermore, one-year prospective results from the PAS cohort validated these low complication and high efficacy outcomes [25]. The S-ICD has also been shown to be safe and highly effective in specialized cohorts, including pediatric populations and those with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [26]. Longitudinal studies of the first-generation S-ICD regulatory cohorts have demonstrated excellent battery longevity exceeding 7 to 8 years [27].

**Integration of Leadless Pacing and Modular Systems**
A primary limitation of S-ICD therapy has been the inability to deliver bradycardia pacing or ATP [21]. To overcome this, investigators designed a communicating, ATP-enabled leadless pacemaker (LP) capable of interacting with the S-ICD using conductive intrabody communication [28]. Recently, the landmark MODULAR ATP trial demonstrated the clinical safety and efficacy of a fully integrated, modular, communicative leadless pacing-defibrillator system [29]. This modular approach represents a paradigm shift, enabling S-ICD patients to receive ATP and backup pacing entirely leadlessly. Early clinical case reports of combined S-ICD and LP implants paved the way for these contemporary systems [30].

**Conclusion**
The S-ICD has matured from a novel alternative into a robust, standard-of-care solution for patients at risk of sudden cardiac death. Recent technological developments, including advanced sensing filters and modular leadless pacing systems, have addressed historical limitations and significantly expanded the clinical utility of S-ICD therapy.
